newsitem.title: GERMANY: German press criticises Bonn, lauds U.S. on taxes.
newsitem.headline: German press criticises Bonn, lauds U.S. on taxes.

text.p: Newspapers on Thursday slammed Germany's political parties for their failure to agree on a major overhaul of the country's tax system, drawing an unfavourable comparison with the United States.
Germany's parliamentary mediation committee voted early on Thursday to reject sweeping government tax reforms aimed at slashing 30 billion marks ($16 billion) in taxes.
This left virtually no chance for them to become law before general elections in 1998. The plan was blocked by opposition parties.
In contrast, a $94 billion five-year tax cut package is expected to pass the U.S. two-chamber legislature later on Thursday.
"There could barely be more contrasting reports on the ability of countries to implement reform," the Handelsblatt business daily said.

"While the U.S. government and congress are agreeing massive tax cuts...linked in to a budget compromise, Bonn politicians have simultaneously allowed the tax reform which was correctly dubbed by all experts as the reform of the century to collapse quietly," the newspaper added.

"The United States, and also a number of our European neighbours, have recognised the signs of the times and are responding in an appropriate manner to the challenges presented by the globalisation of the economy. In the political international competition stakes, Bonn's decision-makers stand defeated yet again at the bottom of the table."

The Boersen-Zeitung business daily commented: "Helmut (Kohl) is a long way from doing what Bill (Clinton) has done....The way it looks now, the tax reform will only occur in the year 2000 even in the most favourable case; that means lost years up until then.
"We would do better to look closely at what the Americans are capable of," it added.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung also noted the contrast in the ability of the two countries to gain political consensus, once thought of as Germany's particular postwar strength.
"Two worlds. With pragmatism and common sense, the Americans have handed themselves a lowering of capital taxes to keep their economy on the upswing.
"In Germany, a tax reform that would have offered a realistic chance of offering hope to the jobless has collapsed on ideological differences," it said.

It was clear which end-result was ultimately more attractive to international investors, it added, commenting: "Where money flows under such conditions is obvious from the strength of the dollar and the weakness of the mark."
For the Munich-published Sueddeutsche Zeitung, the likely failure of the tax reform was further proof of Germany's continued inability to change itself to meet the realities of the late 20th century.

"Germany will for the foreseeable future remain a high-tax country that will scare off investors because they can see that even red-run (Socialist) countries are demonstrating that it can be otherwise," it said.
